doc.title: Tom Malone interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 3, 2023

title: Adapting to changing styles in the studio scene
summary: Malone says musicians must adapt, noting the 1970 shift from big band and jazz to rock and Latin, classical and Hasidic pop work.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: You just said something that I wanted to follow up on. The group of people that I graduated with, we all had aspirations to maybe get in a big band, oh my God if we could get in Buddy Rich’s big band. Most of them took the fall-back position and became public school teachers, which is an honorable, you know, position. But for those of you in that group that had aspirations to be jazz musicians, to have a band, to record for Blue Note, like your musical heroes did, but now you’re playing two, three, four sessions a day and I wonder if that ever got to be like, wow what happened? This is not what I anticipated.

Well you make plans in your life based on what’s going on around you at the time. But everything changes and you have to be willing to change with the style of music. I know when I first got to New York, 1970, the studio recording scene was in a transition from big band and jazz to rock & roll. And there were a lot of guys like bass players, drummers — oh this rock & roll thing’s never going to catch on, I don’t want to play that junk. You know they used a different word. And so, and those guys were out of the business overnight. And there were other guys, like let’s say upright jazz bass player, listened to the rock & roll stuff and says, “I can do that. I can play electric bass. I can play that rock & roll stuff.” And these people continued to be busy players — drummers, bass players, guitar players, you know. So you have to roll with the punches. You have to change with what’s going on. You have to adapt your music skills. I mean it’s still going

to be the same twelve notes. But you have to be able to play jazz, you have to play Latin, you have to play classical, you have to play whatever style of music, you just have to play it. There’s Hasidic pop recordings too, in Brooklyn. Mordechai Ben David, Avraham Fried, all those guys, Yeedle, all of them. They dress up like the Blues Brothers too.
